about: Entries for the news page (news.html). The page shows entries with status 'reviewed'; entries with status 'draft' appear only when the page is opened with ?drafts. Each story: id, title, outlet, date (published, YYYY-MM-DD), url, level (State|District|National), place, roles[], measure, measureCat (Vacancies and openings|Departures|Job postings|Service effects), direction (Improving|Worsening|Mixed|Not stated; Not stated means the story supplies no comparison over time), dirBase (the baseline the direction is relative to), dirLabel (optional full replacement for the direction tag when a story combines a trend with a level), claim, measured, numbers, rate (reported|source|calculated|none), rateType (e.g. Vacancy rate, Fill rate; omit when rate is none), rateText, context, consequences (label each as observed, reported by whom, a concern, or anticipated if adopted; 'None described in the story.' if none), openQuestions ("What else we might want to know": one or two neutral sentences naming information that would help interpret the story and that neither the story nor the added context supplies), sources[] ({label,url} for every figure or definition imported from outside the story); optional stateContext ({text,url}: for stories about one district, or about a state's figures other than its official vacancy data, one sentence on what the state publishes, linking its dashboard entry (index.html#def-XX) if the state is on the dashboard and the inventory (provenance.html#inventory) otherwise; say when it covers different roles), dash (dashboard state id), group (key in groups), sourceType (e.g. 'Union estimates', 'Vendor-sponsored survey', 'District administrative count'); added (date logged), status (draft|reviewed).

stories.title: Providence schools report 30 teacher vacancies ahead of school year
stories.measure: Open positions before school starts
stories.claim: The superintendent reports 30 open teaching positions across 37 schools, with no school missing more than three, about three weeks before school starts.
stories.measured: Early August 2026, about three weeks before the 2026–27 school year
stories.numbers: 30 open teaching positions. The district has more than 1,400 teachers when fully staffed. 103 teachers retired or resigned this year.
stories.rateText: About 2%, using 30 openings and the story's fully staffed complement of more than 1,400 teachers.
stories.context: 71 classroom vacancies on the first day of 2025–26, and at least 100 in each of the six years before that; that comparison pairs this early-August count with earlier first-day counts. Hardest to fill: math, science, and special education.
stories.consequences: None described in the story.
stories.openQuestions: Whether the 30 openings were filled by the first day, and how this count compares with the state's own vacancy data for the district, which RIDE publishes.

stateContext.text: Rhode Island publishes current unfilled positions by district but no rate (Providence: 87 when this project's inventory was compiled, a different date from the story's).

stories.title: WCCUSD students return to nearly fully staffed schools
stories.measure: Vacancies on the first day
stories.claim: District officials report 37 teaching vacancies on the first day of school, the lowest in recent memory; the teachers union credits a new contract.
stories.measured: First day of the 2026–27 school year (Aug. 18, 2026)
stories.numbers: 37 vacancies (12 elementary, 13.4 middle and high school, the rest special education); 89 new teachers hired.
stories.rateText: 2.6% of teaching positions, according to district officials.
stories.context: About 70 vacancies at the start of last year and about 100 the year before; the union credits a raise of roughly 8%. Separately, the district cut about 10% of its workforce under a three-year plan to close a budget shortfall (Richmondside, June 2026); neither story says how that affected teaching vacancies.
stories.consequences: None described in the story.

sources.label: Richmondside, June 25, 2026: district budget and workforce reduction

stories.openQuestions: How the 2.6% is calculated (which positions, counted on what date), and how many teaching positions the workforce reduction eliminated, which affects how the drop in vacancies should be read.

stateContext.text: California's statewide count measures something different: assignments without a permanently assigned certificated employee on census day.

stories.title: CCSD reports 167 teacher vacancies, support professional openings at 454
stories.measure: Vacancies at the start of the year
stories.claim: The superintendent reports 167 vacancies and a 99% fill rate, with 91 of the openings in special education; support staff openings total 454.
stories.measured: Start of the 2026–27 school year
stories.numbers: 167 vacancies; the story refers to licensed professional openings but does not fully specify which positions the 167 covers. 91 are in special education. Reported separately: 454 support professional openings, 8 nurse vacancies, and a fully staffed school police force.
stories.rateText: 99% filled, as stated by the superintendent, for the positions behind the 167 vacancies; the story does not give their total. It is not an all-staff rate and does not cover the 454 support openings.
stories.context: Fewer vacancies than in previous years, without figures. Total employment is lower than in each of the last two years, which some attribute to declining enrollment.
stories.consequences: None described from vacancies. Smaller classes at one middle school are attributed to lower enrollment.
stories.openQuestions: Which positions the 167 vacancies and the 99% cover and how many such positions there are, and earlier years' counts behind the comparison with previous years.

stateContext.text: Nevada publishes teacher vacancies, but their timing is unclear; the state is a candidate for the dashboard, not yet shown.

stories.title: Teacher vacancies drop in Washoe County and Carson City
stories.place: Washoe County and Carson City school districts, Nevada
stories.measure: Open positions before school starts
stories.claim: District HR officials report about 50 open teaching positions in Washoe County, about 30 of them in special education, and three paraprofessional vacancies in Carson City.
stories.measured: Summer 2026, heading into 2026–27; the official notes the count changes quickly
stories.numbers: Washoe: about 50 open teacher positions (about 30 special education, 20 general education). Carson City: 3 paraprofessional vacancies.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The story gives no total positions, and the latest federal count of Washoe's teachers (NCES, 2024–25, in full-time equivalents) is two school years old.
stories.context: Washoe had nearly 300 openings a few years earlier. Officials credit a 2025 state law easing certification for out-of-state teachers.
stories.consequences: A parent says her child's school has no dedicated PE or art teacher, so classroom teachers cover those classes; she ties this to whether parents have raised money for those teachers, not to unfilled funded positions.
stories.openQuestions: The number of teaching positions this fall, whether the 50 openings were filled when school started, and the date of the earlier count of nearly 300.

stateContext.text: Nevada publishes teacher vacancies, but their timing is unclear; the state is a candidate for the dashboard, not yet shown.

sources.label: NCES Common Core of Data, Washoe County School District: 2024–25 teacher count

stories.title: CMS superintendent returns for back-to-school briefing amid investigation
stories.measure: Openings reported before the start of the year
stories.claim: At its back-to-school briefing, the district reports about 160 teacher vacancies and about 100 bus driver openings.
stories.measured: Reported at the Aug. 18, 2026 back-to-school briefing, before school started; the count date is not specified
stories.numbers: About 160 teacher vacancies; about 100 bus driver openings. The district has about 18,000 employees.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The only total given is all district employees, which is not the right denominator for teacher or driver vacancies.
stories.context: No prior-year comparison; vacancies are not defined.
stories.consequences: None described in the story.
stories.openQuestions: How the district defines a vacancy and on what date it counted, the number of teaching and driver positions, and last year's counts at the same point.

stateContext.text: For teachers, North Carolina's education department (DPI) publishes district vacancy rates on a broader measure that includes positions filled by long-term substitutes or provisionally licensed teachers. For bus drivers, the superintendents' association counted 1,278 vacancies statewide in September 2026, a figure it calls soft, with no definition or denominator.

stories.title: Record teacher turnover leaves FWISD with few vacancies, but fewer veteran educators
stories.measure: Departures, plus vacancies before school starts
stories.claim: Public records obtained by the Report show teacher departures rose about 60% in 2025–26; the district reports nine classroom vacancies remaining.
stories.measured: Departures during 2025–26, by effective date; vacancies as of Aug. 6, 2026
stories.numbers: 1,102 teachers resigned or retired in 2025–26, up from 690 the year before; departures of teachers with 10 or more years in the district rose from 136 to 279. 9 classroom vacancies. The superintendent estimated about 350 uncertified teachers.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The story gives no total number of teachers, and with enrollment declining and positions cut, an older federal count would not match.
stories.context: Most departures (942 of 1,102) took effect after the March 24 state takeover, as most did the year before (552 of 690). Effective dates need not show when teachers decided to leave, and a researcher quoted in the story cautions that timing alone does not show the takeover caused the increase. The superintendent says declining enrollment meant not every departure needed replacing.
stories.consequences: Concerns rather than observed effects: a union leader and a university researcher say filling positions does not replace lost experience.
stories.dirLabel: Mixed staffing picture: departures rose; few classroom vacancies remained
stories.openQuestions: The number of teaching positions before and after the cuts, whether departing teachers were replaced or their positions eliminated, and departures in comparable districts not under state control.

stateContext.text: Texas began a statewide teacher vacancy collection in 2026–27; no statewide figures are published yet.

stories.title: After announcing zero vacancies, Fort Worth ISD has dozens of teacher openings
stories.measure: District vacancy count vs. job postings
stories.claim: The district said it started the year with zero classroom teaching vacancies; by late September its job portal listed dozens of openings.
stories.measured: Zero-vacancy figure as of about Aug. 11, 2026; job postings as of Sept. 30, 2026
stories.numbers: Zero core classroom vacancies (August). On Sept. 30: 27 elementary and secondary classroom openings, 7 arts/athletics/health/PE, 4 special education, 9 paraprofessional, and 13 office support, 60 in all.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. No total positions are given, and postings are not the same as vacancies on a fixed date.
stories.context: The zero figure covered core classroom teachers only; specialized roles such as dyslexia teachers and speech-language pathologists were already posted when it was announced.
stories.consequences: Reported by a parent: her son's teachers changed three weeks into the year. The district says it reassigned staff because some classes had more than 35 students and others fewer than 10.
stories.openQuestions: Vacancies across all roles on a fixed date, rather than core classroom positions only, and how many of the September postings were open since the start of the year.

stateContext.text: Texas began a statewide teacher vacancy collection in 2026–27; no statewide figures are published yet.

stories.title: School districts under state control see more teacher vacancies
stories.place: Fort Worth ISD and six other Texas districts under state control
stories.measure: Departures (resignations and notices)
stories.claim: Spectrum News reports that departures rose in Fort Worth and in all six of the eight other state-controlled districts that responded to its request.
stories.measured: Mostly 2025–26 departures; windows differ by district (for example, April–June notices in Beaumont)
stories.numbers: Fort Worth: more than 1,000 departures, with notices from March to June up 72%. Houston: 1,622 resignations this past year, below a peak of 2,810 but above the 1,050 before the takeover. Beaumont: 219 notices from April to June, up 86%.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The figures are departure counts without total staff, and the districts' windows and definitions may differ.
stories.context: The headline refers to vacancies, but the figures are departures. Comparisons are within each district over time, with windows that differ; there is no comparison group of districts not under state control.
stories.consequences: Reported by a parent: her child lost a speech-language pathologist in the district's redesign. Two Fort Worth board members said the district failed to have its speech-language pathology team fully staffed at the start of the year and apologized. Those positions were outside the district's earlier count of zero classroom vacancies.
stories.dirBase: vs. before takeover; Houston below its peak

sources.label: Fort Worth Star-Telegram (via Yahoo News), Sept. 30, 2026: the zero-vacancy count covered core classroom positions only

stories.openQuestions: Total staff in each district, so departures can be read as rates; the same figures for districts not under state control; and whether departures were replaced.

stateContext.text: Texas began a statewide teacher vacancy collection in 2026–27; no statewide figures are published yet.

stories.title: Illinois teacher vacancies down nearly 25% in 2025
stories.measure: Unfilled positions on Oct. 1 (state collection)
stories.claim: Reporting ISBE's annual collection, the story says unfilled teaching positions fell 24% and describes the state's Teacher Vacancy Grant, which ISBE credits for the decline.
stories.measured: Oct. 1, 2025 (2025–26 school year)
stories.numbers: 2,943 unfilled teaching positions, down from 3,864; 1,079 in special education. Also unfilled: 2,134 paraprofessional, 964 school support, and 167 administrative positions.
stories.rateText: ISBE gives a teacher vacancy rate of 2.1%, down from 2.76%; the story reports counts only. The 24% decline refers to the count.
stories.context: Under ISBE's definition, positions covered by a substitute without a permanent holder count as unfilled.
stories.consequences: None described in the story.
stories.openQuestions: How much of the decline reflects positions filled rather than positions eliminated, and how unfilled positions are spread across districts.

stories.title: Iowa teacher shortage shows improvement with 99% of positions filled
stories.measure: Postings over 12 months, unfilled or filled by substitutes
stories.claim: Citing the Iowa Department of Education, the story reports nearly 99% of full-time teaching positions filled and describes Iowa's rate as three times better than the national average.
stories.measured: Postings from August 2024 to August 2025; the state labels the figure 2025–26
stories.numbers: Nearly 99% of full-time teaching positions filled. The state's release gives 434 unfilled positions, 1.15% of full-time teachers.
stories.rateText: Nearly 99% filled, as the story reports. That figure corresponds to the state's measure of 434 unfilled postings, 1.15% of full-time teachers employed: a year's unfilled postings relative to employed teachers, not a point-in-time share of authorized positions filled.
stories.context: The state's release compares Iowa's 1.15% with NCES's 3% national figure. The two use different measurement windows and definitions (a year of postings vs. an October snapshot of vacant positions), so they are not directly comparable. The teachers union says the metric ignores positions and courses districts have cut.
stories.consequences: None described in the story.
stories.rateType: Share of positions filled, as reported

sources.label: Iowa Department of Education release, Jan. 5, 2026

stories.openQuestions: How many positions districts cut or left unposted, which the teachers union says the measure misses, and a point-in-time vacancy count comparable with other states'.

stories.title: S.C. teacher vacancies drop as alternative certification program grows
stories.measure: Vacancies at the start of the school year (district survey of teaching and certified service positions)
stories.claim: Citing an unnamed recent report, the story says districts reported 706 teacher vacancies at the start of 2025–26, down about 30% from just over 1,000.
stories.measured: Fall 2025 snapshot (start of 2025–26); news story published September 2026
stories.numbers: 706 vacancies, versus just over 1,000 the year before. The 706 is CERRA's total for teaching (548.55) and certified service positions such as counselors and librarians (157.68); the story calls them teacher vacancies. 74 of 75 districts reported in 2025–26, versus 71 the year before.
stories.rateText: 1.23% for teaching and certified service positions combined: 706.23 vacant ÷ (56,521.19 filled + 706.23 vacant), from CERRA's tables. For teaching positions alone: 548.55 ÷ (51,345.99 + 548.55) = 1.06%.
stories.context: The story does not name the report; the figures match CERRA's 2025–26 supply and demand tables. An alternative certification program says more than 300 of its teachers entered classrooms this school year (apparently 2026–27, a year after the vacancy count); its retention claim is the program's own figure.
stories.consequences: None described in the story.

sources.label: CERRA 2025–26 Educator Supply & Demand data tables

stories.openQuestions: Which report the story cites, and the 2026–27 count, since these figures describe the previous school year.

stories.title: Left on the curb: How NYC's paraprofessional shortage leaves some students with disabilities stranded
stories.measure: Union estimate of vacancies
stories.claim: The teachers union estimates about 1,600 paraprofessional vacancies citywide and says the shortage leaves some students with disabilities without required services.
stories.measured: Not stated
stories.numbers: About 1,600 paraprofessional vacancies and about 26,000 paraprofessionals citywide, both union estimates. Salaries range from $34,000 to $57,000; new paras start as substitutes at $188 a day.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The 26,000 may count employed paraprofessionals rather than all positions, and neither union figure is dated or defined.
stories.context: The story provides no official city vacancy count. A comptroller's audit found complaints about the bus hotline rose sharply between 2021 and 2023–24.
stories.consequences: Reported by a parent: her son, whose education plan requires a bus paraprofessional, missed more than half of 2024–25 and about a quarter of the following year when no para was available, and getting one assigned took months.
stories.openQuestions: An official, dated count of paraprofessional vacancies and positions, and how many students missed required services.

stateContext.text: New York surveys districts about vacancies and hiring, but no statewide figures were found.

stories.title: Northside ISD bus driver shortage leaves Northwest San Antonio families scrambling at the start of school
stories.measure: Unfilled transportation positions
stories.claim: The district's transportation director reports more than 70 unfilled transportation positions.
stories.measured: About Aug. 20, 2026, in the first weeks of 2026–27
stories.numbers: More than 70 unfilled positions: more than 30 drivers requiring a commercial license, more than 20 other drivers, and more than 20 bus monitors.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The story gives no total number of drivers, monitors, or routes.
stories.context: No prior-year comparison. The district says new hires could be driving within four to six weeks.
stories.consequences: The district says drivers are running double routes, lengthening trips. Reported by a parent: late or missed pickups since the first day.
stories.openQuestions: The number of driver and monitor positions and routes, how many routes are doubled and how late buses run, and last year's count.

stateContext.text: Texas's new statewide collection covers teaching positions, not bus drivers, and no figures are published yet.

stories.title: Albemarle schools make progress on bus driver shortage ahead of first day
stories.measure: Open bus routes
stories.claim: The district reports six open bus routes before the first day, down from nine open driver positions earlier in the summer, with substitutes covering all six.
stories.measured: About Aug. 10, 2026, before the first day of school
stories.numbers: 6 open routes (earlier: 9 open positions); 4 new drivers trained and 6 in training; starting pay $24.43 an hour, up from $23.76.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. No total number of routes or drivers is given, and the earlier figure counts positions while the later one counts routes.
stories.context: The district raised pay, paid for commercial license training, and held a hiring fair.
stories.consequences: None described; the district says substitutes cover all open routes and drivers can double up if needed.
stories.openQuestions: The total number of routes, and how many were open at the same point last year.

stories.title: After-school sports take a back seat as Michigan school bus driver shortages persist
stories.measure: Descriptions of service cuts
stories.claim: The state's pupil transportation association says districts short of drivers are putting home-to-school routes ahead of after-school trips.
stories.measured: Fall 2026; the national survey covers the past one to two years
stories.numbers: No counts for Michigan. National context (vendor survey): a survey by HopSkipDrive, a student transportation company, reports that 71% of responding district administrators had at least one disruption from driver shortages in the past year, and about 78% took steps such as consolidating runs or raising pay.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The story gives no counts of drivers, positions, or routes for Michigan.
stories.context: A former driver says pay rules discourage extra trips, such as paying waiting time less than driving time.
stories.consequences: Described by the state transportation association: some athletic conferences have moved game times later, neighboring districts share buses, and schools have asked parents to carpool and coaches to get commercial licenses. Neither these accounts nor the national survey show how widespread this is in Michigan.
stories.openQuestions: Counts of driver vacancies or canceled trips in Michigan, and how widespread the described changes are.

stateContext.text: Michigan's statewide vacancy data cover teaching positions, not bus drivers.

stories.title: Parents concerned CMS bus driver shortage could lead to bell schedule changes at multiple campuses next school year
stories.measure: Proposed schedule changes; no counts
stories.claim: Parents say a bus driver shortage is behind a proposal to change bell times at several schools starting in 2027–28, including moving one magnet school's day an hour later; the district describes the proposal as part of an annual transportation efficiency review.
stories.measured: Proposal discussed in October 2026, for the 2027–28 school year
stories.numbers: No counts of driver vacancies, drivers, or routes. The named magnet school would start at 9:15 a.m. and dismiss at 4:15 p.m., an hour later than now.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The story gives no driver or route counts.
stories.context: A district transportation official says the focus is on filling vacant driver positions. In August the district reported about 100 bus driver openings (see related coverage).
stories.consequences: Anticipated if adopted, according to parents: the later schedule would conflict with work hours, and parents estimate up to half of the magnet school's families could consider changing schools.

sources.label: WBTV, Aug. 18, 2026: about 100 bus driver openings

stories.openQuestions: The current number of driver vacancies and routes, and how the proposal would change routes and ride times.

stateContext.text: North Carolina's superintendents' association counted 1,278 bus driver vacancies statewide in September 2026, a figure it calls soft; it publishes no definition or denominator.

stories.title: Maryland officials announce dramatic decrease in teacher vacancy rate
stories.measure: Teacher vacancies reported by local school systems (state collection)
stories.claim: State officials announced that teacher vacancies fell from 2,145 in 2022–23 to about 572 this school year, and credited recruitment and retention programs.
stories.measured: Current school year (2026–27), announced Oct. 19, 2026; the story does not give the count date. MSDE's annual collection counts vacancies on the first day of school.
stories.numbers: 2,145 vacancies in 2022–23; about 572 now. Anne Arundel County: 283 in 2022 and 16 on the first day of school in August 2026. Maryland has more than 64,000 educators.
stories.rateType: Vacancy rate (as reported; base not stated)
stories.rateText: About 0.9% of teaching positions in 2026–27, down from about 3.4% in 2022–23, as the story reports. Neither the story nor MSDE's release specifies the denominator or its date, and the rounded percentages do not establish how the rates were calculated. The dashboard's approximate same-school-year calculation for 2022–23 (first-day vacancies divided by vacancies plus October teachers) is 3.31%; it has no rate for 2026–27 yet.
stories.context: The story calls the drop roughly 70%; the counts give 73.3%, the figure in MSDE's release. The Banner noted that some districts cut positions this year (Baltimore County about 600, half of them teaching jobs; Montgomery County 415), leaving fewer openings to fill, while Anne Arundel County reduced vacancies without cuts or layoffs; the state board president said a full report on causes is due later this year. The story also notes that some federal workers who lost jobs have moved into teaching. Other coverage of the same announcement: The Banner, WMAR, Southern Maryland Chronicle, and a Times-News reprint.
stories.consequences: None described in the story.

sources.label: MSDE release, Oct. 19, 2026: counts and 73.3% decline
MSDE, Maryland's Teacher Workforce (Feb. 2026): first-day vacancy collection
The Banner, Oct. 19, 2026: district position cuts, Anne Arundel without cuts, and pending state report
Southern Maryland Chronicle, Oct. 20, 2026: same announcement

stories.openQuestions: The count date for the 572 and how the reported rates were calculated, the October 2026 teacher count needed for a same-year rate, and how many positions districts cut, which the state board's coming report may address.

stories.title: New data: NC teacher vacancies fell before new pay raise
stories.measure: Vacancies reported by all 115 districts at the start of the school year (NC School Superintendents' Association survey)
stories.dirLabel: Mixed staffing picture: teacher vacancies fell; total vacancies rose slightly
stories.claim: The story reports that teacher vacancies at the start of 2026–27 fell to 2,009, the fewest in at least six years, while total vacancies across all job categories rose slightly to 6,265, the first increase since the association began publishing a statewide total in 2022.
stories.measured: Start of 2026–27: the association's survey is a snapshot as of Sept. 21, 2026, released Sept. 24; story published Sept. 30.
stories.numbers: Teacher vacancies 2,009 (down 6.8%), including 569 exceptional children teachers (down 10%); elementary 601 (up 3.3%). Total 6,265, up from 6,210. Classified staff 2,419 (up 8.9%); bus drivers 1,278 (up 4.5%), a figure the association calls soft because some districts hire drivers who also work as teacher assistants; counselors, psychologists, and social workers 171 (down 26%). 5,459 residency-licensed teachers (up 5.3%). 12 districts reported no teacher vacancies.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available for the association's counts, which have no denominator. The 7.4% the story cites is for a different measure: the state education department's 2025–26 count on the 40th school day, which also treats positions filled by long-term substitutes or teachers without full licenses as vacant.
stories.context: The association's release gives 2,009.1 teacher vacancies, including 568.5 in exceptional children. Its director attributes last year's larger drop to districts cutting positions paid for by federal pandemic funds, which ended in 2024. The headline says vacancies fell before the new pay raise; the story notes that the budget raising pay (effective July 1) was signed July 7, after most districts had finished fall hiring. The Sept. 21 snapshot came after both dates, and the story does not show when the decline occurred or rule out an effect of the expected raise on hiring. Carolina Journal is published by the John Locke Foundation, a policy group; the story also quotes the foundation's education director, who expects the raise to keep vacancies falling. The News & Observer covered the same release on Sept. 24 (free copy via Yahoo News), giving last year's total as 6,209.
stories.consequences: None described in the story. The association's director said that more than 6,200 vacancies, especially for classified staff and bus drivers, show staffing challenges remain (a concern).

sources.label: NCSSA release, Sept. 24, 2026: snapshot date and unrounded counts
News & Observer (via Yahoo News), Sept. 24, 2026: same release

stories.openQuestions: The number of positions in each category, to put the counts in proportion; how many vacancies are covered by substitutes; and whether the rise in classified and driver vacancies reflects more positions or fewer hires.

stateContext.text: North Carolina's education department (DPI) also publishes statewide and district vacancy rates, but its measure counts positions filled by long-term substitutes or provisionally licensed teachers as vacant, so the dashboard does not use it.

stories.title: What CMS staff is proposing to make bus routes, transportation more efficient
stories.measure: Drivers running routes on a given day vs. drivers needed
stories.claim: The story reports that about 640 drivers run routes on a given day, against the 750 the district needs, and describes a staff proposal to shift bell times at seven campuses next school year.
stories.measured: Reported Oct. 20, 2026; the date of the on-a-given-day figure is not specified
stories.numbers: About 640 drivers on a given day; 750 needed. 101,000 of 141,000 students ride the bus. Seven campuses would change bell times, including one magnet school moving from 8:15 a.m.–3:15 p.m. to 9:15 a.m.–4:15 p.m.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The 640 counts drivers working on a given day, which may reflect absences and other coverage constraints as well as vacancies, and the 750 is a stated need rather than a count of positions.
stories.context: In August the district reported about 100 bus driver openings (see related coverage). The decision rests with district operations staff; a board member placed the proposal on the next week's board agenda.
stories.consequences: Anticipated if adopted, according to parents: a parent cites a survey (its sponsor is not stated) in which 49% of respondents said they may withdraw their children, and warns that lower enrollment would reduce funding and teachers. A board member says the district is looking for more efficient routes and hopes for a compromise.

sources.label: WBTV, Aug. 18, 2026: about 100 bus driver openings

stories.openQuestions: How many driver positions are funded and vacant, as distinct from drivers working on a given day; how ride times would change under the proposal; and who conducted the parent survey.

stateContext.text: North Carolina's superintendents' association counted 1,278 bus driver vacancies statewide in September 2026, a figure it calls soft; it publishes no definition or denominator.

stories.title: LOCAL 3 INVESTIGATES: Lawmakers could reverse bus driver age law passed after Woodmore tragedy
stories.measure: Route changes and early dismissals; no counts
stories.claim: The story reports that Sequatchie County Schools changed bus routes several times this fall because of a driver shortage, including sending students home early so buses could run multiple routes.
stories.measured: Late September and Oct. 2, 2026, during 2026–27
stories.numbers: No counts of drivers, vacancies, or routes. On Oct. 2 some students were dropped off about two hours early.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The story gives no counts of drivers, positions, or routes.
stories.context: The story is about a bill to lower Tennessee's minimum school bus driver age from 25 to 23, which passed the Senate and stalled in the House; its sponsor calls the shortage a crisis. The story describes Sequatchie County as an outlier and says most Chattanooga-area systems are not actively short of drivers.
stories.consequences: Observed, from the district's announcements as described in the story: students sent home early in late September and dropped off about two hours early on Oct. 2, with families arranging their own transportation if they wanted a full day.

stories.title: Berkeley County schools hold hiring fair for bus drivers, teachers
stories.place: Berkeley County School District, South Carolina
stories.measure: Open positions cited ahead of a district hiring fair
stories.claim: Ahead of its hiring fair, the district cites 21 classroom vacancies, 8 in special education, and 20 open transportation positions, and calls bus drivers its top need.
stories.measured: Reported Oct. 22, 2026; the count date is not specified
stories.numbers: 21 classroom vacancies; 8 in special education (the story does not say whether these are part of the 21); 20 open transportation positions, with bus drivers described as the top need.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The story gives no total positions for any role.
stories.context: A district hiring specialist says some transportation staff were hired after vacancies opened at the start of the year. The next day, WCIV reported 37 bus driver vacancies from the district; neither story explains the difference between the counts.
stories.consequences: None described in the story.

sources.label: WCIV (ABC News 4), Oct. 23, 2026: 37 bus driver vacancies

stories.openQuestions: Whether the 20 transportation openings and WCIV's 37 driver vacancies count the same positions, whether the 8 special education vacancies are part of the 21, and the total positions for each role.

stateContext.text: South Carolina's statewide rate for teaching positions was 1.06% at the start of 2025–26 (CERRA; 1.23% including certified service positions such as counselors). The state data do not cover bus drivers.

stories.title: Berkeley County parents frustrated as school bus delays, missed stops continue
stories.place: Berkeley County School District, South Carolina
stories.measure: Bus driver vacancies (district count), plus service effects
stories.claim: Parents describe long waits, skipped stops, and late arrivals more than two months into the year; the district reports 37 bus driver vacancies and three Hanahan routes making double runs.
stories.measured: Reported Oct. 23, 2026, during 2026–27; the count date is not specified
stories.numbers: 37 bus driver vacancies districtwide, "including 10" at the Goose Creek transportation facility; two vacancies are assigned to Hanahan routes (the story does not say whether these are among the 10). Three Hanahan routes making double runs. Seven concerns to the Hanahan transportation office this year.
stories.rateText: No comparable rate available. The story gives no total number of drivers or routes.
stories.context: The station first reported the district's transportation problems in August. One parent says problems have worsened this year; the story gives no earlier counts. A Live 5 story the day before cited 20 open transportation positions (see related coverage).
stories.consequences: Documented by the district: three routes making double runs, and some app notifications delayed or missed; it says substitutes on unfamiliar routes can contribute to missed stops. Reported by parents: children waiting about two hours and arriving after 10 a.m., a skipped stop, and a student missing first-period math. Parents also reported three or four students to a seat; the district said it follows state capacity rules but did not confirm.
stories.openQuestions: The number of drivers and routes, how many routes run late or double, and whether conditions are worse than last year, as one parent says.

stateContext.text: South Carolina's statewide vacancy data (CERRA) cover teaching and certified service positions, not bus drivers.
